question: An incident write-up drafted for engineers now has to go to a board audience with no technical background. The draft refers to internal components by their codenames. Which two edits best adapt it for those readers? Select two.
options: A) Replace component codenames with a plain account of what customers experienced.
B) Add a glossary of the technical terms so the original wording can all be retained.
C) Open with the decision the board is being asked to make and what it depends on.
D) Shorten every sentence to under fifteen words so the document reads more quickly.
E) Keep the minute-by-minute chronology, since that is how the incident really unfolded.
correct_answers: A) Replace component codenames with a plain account of what customers experienced.
C) Open with the decision the board is being asked to make and what it depends on.
explanations: Correct. Board readers cannot evaluate internal codenames, but they can weigh what customers experienced. Describing the impact in plain terms gives them something they can act on, which the codenames alone do not.
A glossary preserves the engineering framing and asks the board to do the translation, which is the work the author should be doing for them.
Correct. Reordering for the reader's purpose is a separate change from translating the vocabulary: the board needs the decision first, not after the narrative.
A mechanical sentence-length rule chops explanation into fragments and does nothing about the underlying content being framed for the wrong audience.
An accurate chronology is still the wrong structure here. It buries impact and decisions inside a timeline the board has no reason to follow.
